title: From IM-1 milestone to FY26 inflection guide
body:
## A Blank-Cheque Beginning

When Intuitive Machines completed its merger with Inflection Point Acquisition Corp. in February 2023 and began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker LUNR, the market was buying something unusual: a company with a handful of NASA contracts, a lander prototype, and a thesis — that the United States government's return to the Moon would be executed, in part, by a twelve-year-old Houston startup staffed by former NASA engineers.

The financial profile at listing was characteristically pre-scale for a SPAC target. Revenue was a series of NASA cost-plus and milestone-based contract payments; the company had not yet flown a mission, and the milestone-payment recognition model meant that most of the financial story would be written later. The institutional anchor was the CLPS programme relationship — a framework that gave Intuitive Machines a procurement channel but not a guaranteed income stream. What the de-SPAC actually delivered was a public balance sheet to fund the Nova-C lander programme through to mission execution and a liquid stock currency that would eventually fund the Lanteris transaction. Michael Blitzer's Inflection Point sponsored the vehicle and joined the board; his Kingstown Capital roots brought a shareholder-activist sensibility to a board that otherwise skewed deeply toward government-and-defence credentials.

## The 2023 Revenue Print: Promising, Lumpy, Inconclusive

Through 2023, Intuitive Machines delivered the kind of quarterly revenue prints that characterise NASA milestone-based operators: modest, irregular, and resistant to extrapolation. The company was in mission-preparation mode for IM-1 — procuring payloads, integrating customer instruments, and completing lander acceptance testing. Revenue recognition followed programme milestones rather than time elapsed, which produced an uneven cadence that frustrated any attempt to construct a clean run-rate model.

The CLPS framework — under which NASA effectively purchases delivery services rather than specifying hardware — meant that revenue arrived in tranches: at contract award, at integration milestones, and, critically, at mission completion. For a company flying its first mission, the latter category was still theoretical in 2023.

## February 22, 2024: The Malapert Moment

The quarter that changed everything was Q1 2024. On February 15, 2024, Intuitive Machines launched the Nova-C lander 'Odysseus' — mission designation IM-1 — aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Kennedy Space Center. Seven days later, on [February 22](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026019865/lunr-20251231.htm), Odysseus touched down near the Malapert A crater at the lunar south pole, becoming the first privately-built spacecraft to soft-land on the Moon and the first American-built spacecraft to do so since Apollo 17 in December 1972.

The stock reaction was sharp and immediate. LUNR shares surged as the landing was confirmed, the price move reflecting not just mission success but the repricing of a binary risk: until that moment, a lunar landing by a private operator was an unproven proposition. Post-landing, Intuitive Machines held a demonstrated capability that no other private entity could claim.

The operational complications were disclosed promptly. A landing-leg failure caused Odysseus to come to rest on its side, partially obscuring solar panels and compressing the operational mission window. Despite the anomaly, IM-1 transmitted data and Intuitive Machines was able to claim milestone completion, triggering the associated revenue recognition. Altemus characterised the mission as a historic achievement even in its imperfect form — the landing itself was the proof point the programme required.

## FY24: The First Mission-Era Print

The FY24 full-year results reflected IM-1 revenue recognition flowing through the income statement. The milestone-payment model meant that revenue associated with IM-1 was recognised partly in the year of mission execution, creating a substantially larger FY24 revenue figure relative to the pre-mission 2023 baseline. Gross margins remained challenged, reflecting the early-stage cost structure of a company that had never built and flown a production lander at scale before.

The stock-volatility pattern that would define LUNR's trading character was established in this period: sharp spikes around mission events, followed by consolidation as investors processed the underlying operating-profitability trajectory. Revenue was real; sustained profitability was deferred.

## IM-2 'Athena' and the FY25 Cadence

The IM-2 mission — 'Athena' — launched in early 2025 carrying a complement of NASA science instruments and commercial cargo. The lander reached the lunar surface in Q1 2025, repeating both the achievement and the complications of its predecessor: Athena touched down but encountered operational difficulties on the surface. The pattern reinforced a consistent observation: Intuitive Machines could reliably deliver hardware to the Moon, but the precision of surface operations at the class of the Nova-C lander remained technically demanding.

For the FY25 financial cadence, the IM-2 mission was the primary revenue-generation event of the first half. But the year's quarterly progression illustrated the structural feature that defines milestone-payment operators: [Q4 2025 revenue of $44.8 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000119312525263400/d17822dex991.htm) — down approximately 18 per cent year-on-year — was not a signal of deteriorating commercial momentum. It was the arithmetic of a company that had already recognised the bulk of its deliverable revenue from in-flight programmes, and whose next large recognition event resided in missions still in preparation.

| Period | Revenue | Gross Margin | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025 (full year) | $250M–$300M | — | Lumpy milestone recognition; IM-2 primary event |
| Q4 2025 | $44.8M | 19% | −18% YoY; post-IM-2 inter-mission trough |
| FY2026E (guidance) | $900M–$1B | — | ~3–4× growth; Lanteris contribution + CLPS ramp |

Peter McGrath, who had joined as CFO in September 2024 following a 31-year Boeing career spanning structural analysis, Phantom Works, and launch services, was explicit with investors about the recognition dynamic. The FY25 full-year range of $250–$300 million represented genuine commercial traction — a company that had executed two lunar missions and collected milestone payments from NASA and commercial customers — but the quarterly lumpiness required investors to think in mission cycles rather than calendar quarters. The 19 per cent gross margin in Q4 2025, while thin, marked a progression from the near-zero margins of the pre-mission period and confirmed that the delivery model, imperfect as it was operationally, was generating economics above cost of revenue.

## Lanteris: The Structural Bet

Against this backdrop, the Lanteris Space Systems acquisition — announced ahead of the FY25 full-year print — was the most consequential event in Intuitive Machines' post-SPAC history. The [$800 million transaction](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001844452/000162828026027026/lunr-20251231annualreportf.pdf) ($450 million cash, $350 million stock) brought Boeing Satellite Systems-grade engineering capability into a company that had, until that moment, been a single-product lunar-delivery operator.

Chris Johnson — who had led Lanteris and before that served as President of Boeing Satellite Systems International for more than two decades — was named President of Lanteris Space Systems within Intuitive Machines, effective January 2026. The board rationale was unambiguous: the Lanteris product line extended the addressable market from lunar surface delivery into satellite manufacturing and broader space systems, the portfolio of a prime contractor rather than a mission-logistics specialist.

The structural consequence for backlog was equally clear. Total backlog post-Lanteris stood at $943 million. The NASA CLPS contract ceiling had been expanded to $4.82 billion, with $150 million guaranteed near-term. The IM-5 task order — $180.4 million, the largest single CLPS task order awarded to date — directed seven science and technology payloads to the Lunar South Pole aboard the larger cargo-class Nova-D lander, a material step up from the Nova-C flown on IM-1 and IM-2, signalling both NASA's confidence in the platform and its intent to use Intuitive Machines for progressively more complex surface operations.

## The FY26 Inflection: What $900M Actually Means

The FY26 guidance of $900 million to $1 billion in revenue — implying approximately 3–4 times FY25 — is not primarily an organic growth story. It is an acquisition story with an organic underlayer. The Lanteris contribution, once the Q1 2026 close completed, added a recurring revenue base in satellite systems that the legacy lunar-delivery business could not have generated independently on that timeline. The CLPS task-order ramp — including IM-3, IM-4, and the IM-5 Nova-D mission — provided the organic component.

The critical marker embedded in the guidance is the Adjusted EBITDA target: positive. Since the de-SPAC in February 2023, Intuitive Machines had been a cash-consuming organisation — funding lander development, mission execution, and acquisition integration. The FY26 positive Adjusted EBITDA target is the company's first commitment to operating-level profitability and the signal that management believes the combined entity is crossing from venture-scale capital consumption to self-sustaining commercial operation.

The path to that inflection requires Lanteris integration to proceed without material cost overruns, CLPS task orders to be awarded and executed on schedule, and NASA's Artemis programme to sustain the political and budgetary support that underpins the entire commercial lunar economy. Each condition carries execution risk. What Intuitive Machines had established by May 2026, across three years of post-SPAC life, was that the foundational technical risk — the question of whether a private operator could land on the Moon — had been answered twice over. The financial risk of converting that capability into a profitable space-prime business remained the open question as the company entered the most consequential fiscal year of its short public history.
